source.title: How to Start Training: The Effect of Initialization and Architecture

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Experiments compare initialization and architecture effects on early training, using epochs to a test-accuracy threshold rather than training classification error.
record.gate_note: Training results are reported for reaching 20% test accuracy on MNIST. Figure-only training values are not numerically recoverable from the text. Activation-length measurements in Figures 1, 2 and 4 are not rows because they do not measure training speed or classification error.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4 through initialization comparisons and finite-width qualifications in plain ReLU networks, measuring epochs to 20% MNIST test accuracy rather than final training error.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors prove initialization and architecture conditions controlling activation-length means and variances, and empirically show that these predict early training. Their conclusions concern starting training, not final convergence or near-zero training error.
record.recipe_differences: Tests initialization and architecture effects on early MNIST training, measuring epochs to a test-accuracy threshold rather than training classification error on CIFAR benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization variance, residual-module scales, depth, and layer widths affect the reported startup behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling residual modules predicts early MNIST training performance, with a substantial difference between geometric scales b=0.9 and b=0.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-module scaling controls activation growth and the ability of deep, narrow residual ReLU networks to begin training.

record.problems: The training evidence measures epochs to 20% test accuracy on MNIST, not training classification error. Numerical training values appear only in figures; uncertainty estimates are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: No other training-result rows were omitted. Activation-length results in Figures 1(a), 2(a), and 4 were excluded because they measure activation scale rather than training behavior named by the versions.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, including corrupted or random labels.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious-minimum frequencies, and adding one or two student neurons.
Training-error comparisons between plain batch-normalized convolutional networks and identity-shortcut networks; very deep tanh networks; Fixup.

Gradient propagation measurements, later convergence, orthogonal-versus-Gaussian training comparisons, very deep tanh networks, and training 10,000-layer convolutional networks. Convolutional experiments measure initial activation lengths only.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature adaptation, catapult recovery, and edge-of-stability training.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text supports qualitative training comparisons without recoverable numerical epoch values. The study is not an original source for V4. Activation-length results alone do not establish training-speed effects.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report training classification error, CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100 training results, or corrupted and random-label results.
No teacher-student two-layer ReLU experiment or spurious-minimum frequency is reported.
The paper does not compare plain networks with identity-shortcut networks for depth-related training error, or test normalization removal.

The experiments test He-style initialization, residual-module scaling, and width/depth effects on early MNIST training. They do not test orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, trainable depth at 10,000 layers, or CIFAR classification error.
No above-stability learning-rate or sharpness experiment is reported.

rows.subject: fully connected networks, architecture types (i)–(iv)
rows.size_stated: depth varied; alternating widths 30 and 10, first-half 30 then 10, first-half 10 then 30, or constant width 15

rows.measure: Mean epochs to obtain 20% test accuracy
rows.note: Text says types (i)–(iv) had similar early training dynamics at each fixed depth; training becomes harder with greater depth for constant-width networks. Individual plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: The relevant qualification is that early training becomes harder with depth despite He initialization, which preserves mean activation length. Similar performance across width permutations alone is not evidence of incomplete initialization benefits. Separate architecture and depth conditions.

rows.note: Authors state width-20 networks, which have a lower sum of reciprocal widths, trained faster at every depth than corresponding types (i)–(iv).
rows.check: Width-20 networks train faster than the narrower comparison architectures, but training still becomes harder with depth under He initialization. This supports an architectural qualification, not an observed initialization advantage; initialization is held fixed.
